rows.question: What is the notice period before filing a cheque bounce complaint?
queries: What is the notice period before filing a cheque bounce complaint?
dishonour of cheque for insufficiency of funds notice period demand payment
The Negotiable Instruments Act 1881 section 138 notice
The Negotiable Instruments Act 1881 section 138 proviso b period of thirty days
rows.answer:
The notice demanding payment must be given within thirty days of the receipt of information from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid, and the drawer has a period of fifteen days from the receipt of the notice to make the payment before a complaint can be filed [1][12]. As discussed in the Supreme Court judgment *Kamlesh Kumar versus State of Bihar & Anr.*, after the sending of this notice, fifteen days time is to be given to the noticee from the date of receipt of the said notice to make the payment, and if the noticee fails to do so, the offence is committed and the cause of action for filing the complaint accrues [12].

Conditions and time limits:
- Validity period: The cheque must be presented to the bank within six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier [1].
- Notice period: The demand notice in writing must be given to the drawer within thirty days of the receipt of information by the payee or holder in due course from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid [1].

rows.question: What is presumed about consideration for a negotiable instrument?
queries: What is presumed about consideration for a negotiable instrument?
presumption as to negotiable instruments consideration date time stamp acceptance transfer holder
Negotiable Instruments Act section 118 presumption as to negotiable instruments
Negotiable Instruments Act section 138 presumption in favour of holder
rows.answer:
Every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration, and every such instrument, when it has been accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred, was accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred for consideration under Section 118 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 [1]. 

As explained by the Supreme Court in the case of K.P.O. Moideenkutty Hajee versus Pappu Manjooran and Anr., this presumption is one of law, and upon proof of execution of the instrument, Section 118 imposes a duty on the court to raise a presumption in favour of the holder that the instrument was made for consideration, thereby shifting the burden of proof to the maker of the promissory note to establish a case that it is not supported by consideration [11].

Related provisions:
- Section 43 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, covering a negotiable instrument made, drawn, accepted, indorsed or transferred without consideration [7].

rows.question: When can a contract be avoided if consent was obtained by coercion or misrepresentation?
queries: When can a contract be avoided if consent was obtained by coercion or misrepresentation?
contract voidable on account of coercion fraud misrepresentation
Indian Contract Act section 19 voidability of agreements without free consent
Indian Contract Act section 15 coercion defined
rows.answer:
A contract can be avoided when consent to the agreement is caused by coercion, or by misrepresentation (except when the party whose consent was caused by misrepresentation or fraudulent silence had the means of discovering the truth with ordinary diligence), as provided under Section 19 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1]. 

Conditions and time limits:
- The fraud or misrepresentation must have caused the consent of the party on whom the fraud was practised or to whom the misrepresentation was made [1].
- The contract is not voidable if the party whose consent was caused by misrepresentation or by fraudulent silence had the means of discovering the truth with ordinary diligence [1].

rows.question: Who is competent to enter into a contract?
queries: Who is competent to enter into a contract?
competency to contract age of majority soundness of mind disqualification
Indian Contract Act section 11
Indian Contract Act section 12 unsound mind
rows.answer:
Every person is competent to contract who is of the age of majority according to the law to which they are subject, is of sound mind, and is not disqualified from contracting by any law to which they are subject, as stated in Section 11 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1]. 

- A person is considered of sound mind for the purpose of making a contract if, at the time of making it, they are capable of understanding it and of forming a rational judgment as to its effect upon their interests, according to Section 12 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [2].
- As noted in Supreme Court judgment "In Re: Interplay Between Arbitration Agreements Under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996 and the Indian Stamp Act 1899", a contract entered into by a person explicitly declared as incompetent or who does not fall within the definition of a competent person under Sections 11 and 12, such as a minor or a person of unsound mind, would be void [13].

Related provisions:
- Section 10 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, which states what agreements are contracts and requires them to be made by the free consent of parties competent to contract [7].

rows.answer:
Whoever commits murder shall be punished with death or imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine, under Section 103(1) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which replaced Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code [1][7]. In the Supreme Court judgment Bharatkumar Rameshchandra Barot versus State of Gujarat, the Court upheld the enhancement of sentence to life imprisonment under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code [7].

- Section 101 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 defines murder and its exceptions, replacing Section 300 of the Indian Penal Code [4][10].
- Section 105 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 covers the punishment for culpable homicide not amounting to murder, replacing Section 304 of the Indian Penal Code [3][9].

rows.answer:
A person accused of a non-bailable offence may be released on bail when arrested or detained without warrant by an officer in charge of a police station, or when appearing or brought before a Court other than the High Court or Court of Session, except where there appear reasonable grounds for believing the person has been guilty of an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life, or if the offence is a cognizable offence and the person has a prior conviction for an offence punishable with death, imprisonment for life, or imprisonment for seven years or more, or has been previously convicted on two or more occasions of a cognizable offence punishable with imprisonment for three years or more but less than seven years, under Section 480 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (which replaced Section 437 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973). [1]

Conditions and time limits:
- The court may direct the release on bail of a person otherwise barred under the death, life imprisonment, or prior conviction clauses if such person is a child, a woman, sick, or infirm, under Section 480 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. [1]

rows.answer:
An arbitral award may be set aside by the Court only on the grounds specified in sub-section (2) and sub-section (2A) of Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 [1].

Conditions and time limits:
- An application for setting aside the award may not be made after three months have elapsed from the date on which the party making that application had received the arbitral award or, if a request had been made under Section 33, from the date on which that request had been disposed of by the arbitral tribunal, under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 [1].
- If the Court is satisfied that the applicant was prevented by sufficient cause from making the application within the said period of three months, it may entertain the application within a further period of thirty days, but not thereafter, under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 [1].
- For the Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, the time limit for making the application is six months, and the further extended period upon sufficient cause is sixty days, under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 [1].

rows.question: How is a sale of immovable property defined and completed?
queries: How is a sale of immovable property defined and completed?
sale of immovable property definition and manner of completion transfer of ownership
Transfer of Property Act 1882 section 54 sale how made

topSources: The Transfer of Property Act, 1882 s54

rows.answer:
A sale of immovable property is defined as a transfer of ownership in exchange for a price paid or promised or part-paid and part-promised under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 [1]. 

As explained in the Supreme Court judgment Lucknow Nagar Nigam & Others versus Kohli Brothers Colour Lab. Pvt. Ltd. & Others, in order to constitute a sale, there must be a transfer of ownership from one person to another where all rights and interests possessed by a person are transferred with free consent for a price called consideration, the conveyance has to be regarded in accordance with law, and the transferor cannot retain any part of their interest or right in the property [11].

Conditions and time limits:
- For tangible immovable property of the value of one hundred rupees and upwards, or for a reversion or other intangible thing, the transfer can be made only by a registered instrument under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 [1]. (Note: For the State of Assam, Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 requires registration by an instrument registered in the State of Assam, notwithstanding the Indian Registration Act, 1908 [1].)

Related provisions:
